Determine an optimal number of spatial levels via an elbow heuristic

Source: R/level-selection.R
determine_optimal_levels.Rd

Computes a WSS curve over k=1..K_max using k-means on projected feature coordinates and selects candidate k values around the elbow.

Usage

determine_optimal_levels(
  data_sf,
  max_levels = 12L,
  top_n = 3L,
  sample_n = 1500L,
  set_seed = 123L,
  response_var = NULL,
  predictor_vars = NULL,
  criterion = c("geometric", "morans_i", "combined"),
  select_on = c("all", "split"),
  on_no_elbow = c("na", "warn", "error")
)

Arguments

data_sf

An sf object. Features without a location (an empty point, or a coordinate that is not finite or lies beyond 1e150, as given or once projected) are dropped with a warning. A layer that mixes XY and XYZ (or XYM) geometries is read in x and y, before and after it is reduced to points, since sf reads a layer in the dimension of its first geometry. So is a layer whose geometries carry M (XYM or XYZM), which GEOS refuses. The points a layer is reduced to are read in x and y when they mix dimensions, as those of a layer XYZ throughout that holds points and polygons do.

max_levels

Integer upper bound on levels. Default 12. The sweep also stops at the number of distinct locations (k-means cannot place more centres) and one short of the number of points.

top_n

Integer; how many candidates to return. Default 3. Under criterion = "geometric" the candidate set is the elbow and its two immediate neighbours, so at most 3 values are ever returned no matter how large top_n is; only the model-aware criteria can return more. Under those it also sets the counts scored, the elbow plus or minus max(4, top_n): a top_n above 4 scores more counts, and under "morans_i" one of them can rank first. A count scores the same whichever top_n puts it in the window.

sample_n

Integer; subsample size for speed. Default 1500.

set_seed

Integer RNG seed for the subsample and the k-means++ restarts; restored afterwards. Default 123. The rows are put in coordinate order before either, so the answer does not depend on the order they come in.

response_var

Optional response column name. Read under criterion = "morans_i", which ranks the counts around the elbow by Moran's I of the cell means, and "combined", which reports that statistic beside the elbow's ranking; under "geometric", the default, it is not read. Where it is read it must be numeric or logical (logicals are read as 0/1); a factor or character response raises an error and is never coerced, because the residuals of an OLS fit to arbitrary level codes carry no meaning to test for autocorrelation. Rows where it, or a predictor, is missing or non-finite stay in the WSS sweep and the cells and are left out of Moran's I; a logged warning gives their number.

predictor_vars

Optional predictor column names, read where response_var is. Must be numeric or logical (logicals are read as 0/1); factor/character columns raise an error. Without them the model-aware criteria regress the cell means on an intercept alone, as resolution_profile() does.

criterion

One of "geometric" (default: the elbow and its two neighbours, read off the coordinates alone), "morans_i" (among the candidates around the elbow, the k at which Moran's I of the cell means, or of their regression residuals, is least significant: the count at which neighbouring cells stop resembling each other, not the count that represents the response best), or "combined" (the candidates around the elbow in the order of the WSS curve's log-log sag, the quantity the elbow is read from, with Moran's I of the cell means and its z in the diagnostics; the statistic does not take part in the ranking). Under "morans_i" a warning of class spatialkit_diagnostic_ranking says that the ranking is by a diagnostic of the cell means; its condition carries k (the count ranked first), criterion, first_computable (the first count at which the statistic is finite) and window (the first and last count tried). "morans_i" and "combined" fall back to "geometric", with a warning, when response_var is not given, and with a logged warning when no candidate clears the nine-cell resolution floor described in Details. A response_var or predictor_vars naming a column that is not in data_sf is an error under every criterion. Supplying both response_var and predictor_vars does not change the criterion: under "geometric" neither is read, and a line logged at the INFO level says that "combined" reports Moran's I.

select_on

"all" (default) selects on every point; "split" reads the response on one spatially blocked half of the points only and returns the other half as the set to estimate on, so that the standard errors computed downstream on the chosen cells are not post-selection. The count is still chosen for the whole layer. See "Post-selection inference".

on_no_elbow

What to do when the count is not a finding about the data: the WSS curve has no elbow, the ladder is too short to show one, or there are too few points or locations for a ladder at all. Each choice raises a condition of class spatialkit_no_elbow there, which carries k (the count the chord rule or the ladder gives), sag (the largest log-log sag of the curve; an elbow needs \(\log 1.25\)) and structured = FALSE, so a caller can catch it without matching the message. "na" (default) returns NA_integer_ there, with a warning of that class, and every result under "na" carries the attributes structured (TRUE when the WSS curve has an elbow, FALSE with the NA) and sag, so one test of attr(k, "structured") covers both outcomes. "warn" returns the counts the chord rule or the ladder gives (see Value), with the same warning; its results carry neither attribute. "error" stops with an error of that class. Under the model-aware criteria the candidates are scored around the elbow: with no elbow, "na" and "error" score none, and under "warn" the ladder places that window.

Value

An integer vector of candidate level counts, best first: under the geometric criterion the elbow, then its lower and upper neighbours; under "morans_i" the candidates in the order of \(|z|\), with a warning of class spatialkit_diagnostic_ranking; under "combined" the candidates around the elbow in the order of the sag. When the WSS curve has no elbow it is NA_integer_, with a warning of class spatialkit_no_elbow (under on_no_elbow = "warn" the ladder's choice and its neighbours, with the same warning; see Details), and so it is when the ladder is too short to show an elbow (max_levels of 1 or 2). At the default on_no_elbow = "na" every result carries the attributes structured (TRUE when the WSS curve has an elbow, FALSE with the NA) and sag. A layer with no points is an error, and one with fewer than three points, or with every point on one location, has no ladder: it returns NA under the same rule, and 1 under "warn". k[1] is therefore the top-ranked count, or NA, on every path, and top_n = 1 returns it alone. When criterion != "geometric", an attribute "diagnostics" is attached with per-k Moran's I values (moran_i) and their standardised deviates (moran_z), the WSS curve (wss) with the relative between-restart spread at each k (wss_spread), the number of rising steps on it (wss_bumps), the restart budget (nstart), the geometric elbow the evaluated neighbourhood was drawn around (knee_k), whether the WSS curve has an elbow (structured) and its largest log-log sag (sag), the k at which k-means failed (failed_k; their wss entries are interpolated from the neighbours, not measured) and the k the model-aware pass actually scored (eval_ks, the elbow's neighbourhood). Under "combined" it also carries the WSS of the re-run clustering at those k (wss_eval, the clustering Moran's I is computed on; reported, not ranked on), the rank of the sag of wss that ordered them (combined_rank, named by k; with no elbow every candidate ties and the order is by distance from knee_k) and criterion = "combined"; when "combined" returned the geometric ranking because the elbow is below ten cells, it carries criterion = "geometric" and fallback (the reason) in place of combined_rank. The NA the default returns on a model-aware call whose WSS curve has no elbow (or a ladder too short to show one) carries the attribute too, with what the sweep measured: moran_i and moran_z all NA and eval_ks empty, since no count was scored, knee_k the count the chord rule lands on, and structured = FALSE. When the model-aware path itself falls back to the geometric result (no viable k in the elbow neighbourhood, a neighbourhood that ends at nine cells or fewer, or, under "morans_i", Moran's I computable at no candidate), no diagnostics are available and the attribute is absent; these fallbacks are logged as warnings. Under "combined" a Moran's I computable at no candidate of a neighbourhood that reaches ten cells is not a fallback: the attribute is there, with moran_i and moran_z all NA, and a logged warning says so. The attribute is absent on the NA of a layer with no ladder (fewer than three points, one location, or k-means failing at every k from 2). The geometric path returns an integer vector with no attribute but structured and sag (none under "warn" or "error"); a rising WSS curve is still logged there. With select_on = "split" every path adds a "split" attribute: a list with selection and estimation (integer row positions in data_sf), method and seed. For a full per-level table of criteria, cell support, restart spread and the flat region, see resolution_profile().

Details

The elbow is read on log-log axes, and there may be none. Points with no cluster structure have a WSS curve close to \(c/k\), and the classical rule, the point furthest below the chord from the first to the last k, still finds a "knee" on it on linear axes, at about \(\sqrt{K_{max}}\): 4 at the default max_levels = 12 and 13 at 160, whatever the data. On \(\log k\) against \(\log\) WSS that curve is a straight line, while separated clusters fall faster than it until there is one cell per cluster and like it after, a bend at the cluster count. The elbow is therefore the k whose \(\log\) WSS sags furthest below the straight line joining k = 1 and \(K_{max}\) on those axes, and it counts as one only when the sag is at least \(\log 1.25\) (the WSS a fifth below the power law through the ends). Measured on 60 to 1500 points with ladders to 3–40, uniform layouts over squares, discs, triangles, an L-shape, density gradients and jittered lattices sagged at most 0.16, and two to ten separated clusters at least 0.6 once max_levels passed the cluster count. With no elbow the function returns NA, so that a count which is not a finding is not passed on as one: the result carries structured = FALSE and the largest sag as sag, and a warning of class spatialkit_no_elbow says why. The linear-axis answer there is the ladder's, not the data's: about \(\sqrt{K_{max}}\), 3 or 4 cells at the default, close to one mean for the whole layer, and the warning carries it as k and the largest sag as sag. on_no_elbow = "warn" returns that count all the same, with the same warning, and "error" stops. An elongated extent also bends, at about its aspect ratio, because the first cuts go across its long axis (0.2–0.45 for a 4:1 rectangle); past the threshold that bend is reported as an elbow, and it describes the extent's shape rather than clusters in it. When locations repeat (stations visited many times), the sweep can reach one cell per distinct location, where the WSS is zero (to within \(10^{-12}\) of the total). That k has no place on log axes and is left out of the line, but the fall to zero is the sharpest bend there is: when the rest of the curve has no elbow, the number of distinct locations is the elbow.

Under criterion = "morans_i" or "combined", with a response_var, the geometric WSS elbow is supplemented with Moran's I of the cell means at each candidate k: the cell means are regressed on the cell-mean predictors (on an intercept alone when no predictor_vars are given) and Moran's I is computed on the residuals over each cell's 8 nearest cells. That statistic tests whether neighbouring cells are independent. It does not measure the autocorrelation the cells leave unexplained in the response, and it does not say how well they represent it: on an autocorrelated response it grows as the cells get finer than the range, because neighbouring cells then resemble each other, and it is close to 0 at about 10 to 20 cells whatever the data, where the neighbour graph is nearly complete. "morans_i" prefers the candidate with the smallest \(|z|\), which is the count at which neighbouring cell means stop resembling each other, cells about as wide as the range. Only the elbow's neighbourhood is scored, so the response moves the answer by at most a few cells either side of the geometric elbow. A ranking by Moran's z is a ranking by a diagnostic, not by a count rule, and it is returned with a warning of class spatialkit_diagnostic_ranking that says so and gives the count ranked first, the first count the statistic could be computed at and the counts scored. Measured on 500 points with a response alone and criterion = "morans_i": the first-ranked count was 10 to 13 on 16 of 16 white-noise layers and on 16 of 16 exponential fields (max_levels 40 and 80), and 10 was the first count the statistic could be computed at on all 32. Those layers have no elbow, so their counts are ranked under on_no_elbow = "warn" only; at the default they return NA. select_resolution() refuses the same statistic unless asked with diagnostic = TRUE; here the criterion is asked for by name, so the count is returned and the warning carries the caveat. "combined" does not rank by the statistic: it orders the same counts by the WSS curve's sag and reports Moran's I and its z beside them in the "diagnostics" attribute, with no such warning. Under "geometric", the default, response_var and predictor_vars are not read, whether one or both are given.

To keep memory use and runtime bounded for large max_levels, the initial k-means sweep records only within-cluster sum-of-squares (WSS) without retaining cluster assignments. Moran's I is then evaluated lazily: k-means is re-run only for a focused neighbourhood around the elbow (±4 by default, or ±top_n if larger), so that only the most promising candidate k values incur the cost of the full Moran's I computation. The re-run at each count draws its starts from a stream of its own, seeded before the sweep, so for one set_seed a count gets the same cells, wss_eval and Moran's I in any neighbourhood that holds it, whichever top_n and max_levels set the neighbourhood: a larger top_n adds counts to the neighbourhood and leaves the scores of the others as they were.

The WSS curve is read for its shape, so it is fitted to be smooth. Every point on it is a k-means local optimum, and with a few random restarts the curve mixes level effects with optimisation noise: measured on clustered layouts, a sweep over k = 1..30 at stats::kmeans(nstart = 5) rose at one or two steps in three of five draws, and an earlier form of the elbow rule once selected such a bump. Each k is therefore fitted as the best of 25 restarts seeded by k-means++ (Arthur and Vassilvitskii 2007), the budget at which the gain from further restarts saturates (Fränti and Sieranoja 2019; Steinley 2003 on why the usual handful is not enough). The same sweeps then had no increase at all. A curve that still rises somewhere is reported but not refused: a bumpy curve is uncertain, not unidentified. A logged warning names the number of rising steps, and the model-aware paths return it as wss_bumps in the "diagnostics" attribute beside wss_spread, the relative spread of WSS across the restarts at each k. Because the optimiser changed, a selection made by an earlier version on a curve that had such a bump can differ from the one made now; where the earlier curve was clean, the selection is the same.

The sweep is plain k-means, whatever the regions are built with afterwards. This function has no partition argument: the elbow is a reading of the sum of squares that plain k-means minimises, and the cells behind Moran's z are that partition's. A count returned here says nothing about density-weighted regions; resolution_profile(), whose regions are of that kind by default, scores counts of those.

"morans_i" ranks on the standardised deviate, not on |Moran's I|. Both \(E[I]\) and \(Var[I]\) depend on the number of cells, so \(|I|\) falls as k grows whether or not the finer tessellation is capturing anything. Measured over 300 replicates of a response with no spatial structure, mean \(|I|\) fell monotonically from 0.114 at k = 10 to 0.050 at k = 60 (\(-56\%\)), which made an \(|I|\) ranking prefer the largest candidate for arithmetic reasons alone. Candidates are therefore ordered by \(|z| = |I - E[I]| / \mathrm{sd}(I)\) using the Cliff & Ord regression residual moments. The cell-level residuals are OLS residuals by construction, which is the case those moments are derived for, but the derivation also assumes errors of equal variance, and a cell mean over \(n_j\) points has a variance proportional to \(1/n_j\). Over the same runs \(z\) had mean \(\approx 0\), \(\mathrm{sd} \approx 1\) and a two-sided 5% rejection rate of 0.040–0.057 at every k, and it stayed calibrated on gradient and moderately clustered layouts; with single-point cells next to cells of 70 or more points its mean rose to 0.2–0.34 and its rejection rate to 7–8% at 20 cells. Where structure remains, \(|z|\) mixes its size with the number of cells it is measured on, since \(\mathrm{sd}(I)\) shrinks as cells are added. Both quantities are reported in the "diagnostics" attribute, as moran_i and moran_z.

Resolution floor on the model-aware criteria. Moran's I is computed on cell-level residuals with an 8-nearest-neighbour weight matrix, so it only carries information once there are more than nine cells. At nine or fewer, every cell is a neighbour of every other, the row-standardised weight matrix is complete, and Moran's I collapses to exactly \(-1/(k - 1)\) for any residual vector (a function of k alone). "morans_i" ranks on \(|z|\), not on \(|I|\), and at the floor the residual moments give \(E[I] = I\) and \(\mathrm{Var}[I] = 0\) identically (the algebra holds to \(10^{-16}\)), so the standardised deviate is \(0/0\): it carries no information about the tessellation, and whichever way rounding noise resolves it those candidates would rank first or last on nothing. They therefore return NA and are excluded from the ranking of "morans_i". When no candidate in the elbow neighbourhood clears the floor, the whole call falls back to the geometric ranking and logs a warning that says so. That is the usual outcome well past max_levels = 10: the neighbourhood is the elbow plus or minus max(4, top_n), and on points with no cluster structure the elbow sits near \(\sqrt{K_{max}}\), so the neighbourhood reaches ten cells only from about max_levels = 40. Measured on 1000 uniform points under on_no_elbow = "warn" (at the default they return NA before any window is placed), max_levels of 12, 20 and 30 all fell back, and 40 scored k = 10 and 11 alone. On such a layer resolution_profile(), which scores Moran's z at every level of its ladder, is the model-aware view. Under criterion = "combined", an elbow below ten cells is a count Moran's I cannot score: the geometric ranking is returned, the elbow and its two neighbours, with a logged warning, and the diagnostics record it (see Value). Otherwise "combined" orders the window by the elbow's own log-log sag at each candidate, the candidates below the floor among them. When the WSS curve has no elbow (under on_no_elbow = "warn") the sag is flat, every candidate tied, and the window comes out in order of distance from the count the chord rule lands on, which is the geometric order.

"combined" is the elbow's ranking of the counts around it, best sag first, with Moran's I of the cell means beside it in the diagnostics. It is not an estimate of the number of clusters, and Moran's I does not take part in the ranking. Averaged with the sag, as it was, it put first ten, the lowest count it scores, or the count after it: on a curve with no elbow the sag is flat and the counts below the floor took the last place on its axis, and with an elbow its \(|z|\) is near 0 at the coarsest counts it scores whatever the response. The sag is read off the sweep's WSS curve, the one the elbow is read from, so with an elbow the first count is the elbow and the counts after it come in order of sag; they can differ from the two neighbours "geometric" returns. The k-means re-run at each candidate, whose cells Moran's I is computed on, can land in a different optimum than the sweep; its WSS is reported as wss_eval and does not rank. The response reaches the diagnostics alone: where Moran's I can be computed at no candidate of a window that reaches ten cells (a constant response, too few cells holding a row with one, or too few in the half that select_on = "split" reads), moran_i and moran_z are NA, the log gives the reason at the WARN level, and the counts are ranked as they would be otherwise. Use "geometric" when the cell count should follow the clustering of the points, "morans_i" for a ranking by the diagnostic, and resolution_profile() when the response should drive the count.

Post-selection inference

When the selection reads the response (here, under criterion = "morans_i" with a response), everything estimated afterwards on the chosen cells is estimated on data that already influenced the choice, and its standard errors are post-selection ones: descriptive, not at nominal coverage (Gao, Bien and Witten 2022; Chen and Witten 2023 give the exact selective test for two k-means clusters, the first link of this chain). The exposure is narrower than "the partition was chosen on the response": every partition here is k-means on the coordinates alone, and the response only decides which count is ranked first. It is not zero, because the count determines every cell the downstream standard errors are computed over. Under "combined" the response reaches the diagnostics and not the ranking, which is the same whether or not Moran's I can be computed.

select_on = "split" is sample splitting: the layer is cut into two spatially blocked halves (make_folds(k = 2, method = "block_kfold")), the criteria that read the response (Moran's I on the cell means) read the first half only, and the row positions of both halves come back in the "split" attribute (selection and estimation). The WSS curve and the k-means cells still use every point: they read coordinates alone, and the count is for a tessellation of every point, so it is chosen on that layer's extent and clusters rather than on half of them. Build the tessellation on every point (cells are geometry), but aggregate and fit on data_sf[attr(x, "split")$estimation, ], whose response the selection never saw. That keeps the selection's use of the response out of the estimates, but only as far as the two halves are independent: the split has no buffer, so points near the border between them are correlated with the selection half over the autocorrelation range, and coverage is nominal only when that range is short against the blocks. The price is precision: half the points estimate, and García Rasines and Young (2023) show a contiguous spatial half is less efficient than the exchangeable split the i.i.d. theory assumes, because the two halves are not interchangeable. Two alternatives keep the whole sample: data thinning for count responses (Neufeld et al. 2024) and data fission for Gaussian-like ones (Leiner et al. 2023). Neither is implemented here; the split needs no distributional assumption, which is why it comes first. Under "combined" the split changes only the rows the diagnostics read. Selection on coordinates alone ("geometric", whatever variables are given) is not exposed in this way, and "split" then changes nothing but the attribute.

The estimation rows cover only the estimation half's blocks, while the cells cover the whole layer, so the estimation rows do not fill every cell. A cell inside the selection half gets none and comes back NA; a cell across the border between the halves is estimated from its estimation-half points alone, and its standard error describes that part, not the cell (on 400 simulated fields a nominal 95% interval covered 0.97 in cells inside the estimation half and 0.88 in cells across the border). Count, per cell, how many of its points are estimation rows, and read inferential results only off cells whose points all are.

References

Arthur, D. and Vassilvitskii, S. (2007). k-means++: the advantages of careful seeding. Proceedings of the 18th Annual ACM-SIAM Symposium on Discrete Algorithms, 1027–1035.

Fränti, P. and Sieranoja, S. (2019). How much can k-means be improved by using better initialization and repeats? Pattern Recognition, 93, 95–112. doi:10.1016/j.patcog.2019.04.014

Steinley, D. (2003). Local optima in K-means clustering: what you don't know may hurt you. Psychological Methods, 8(3), 294–304. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.8.3.294

Gao, L. L., Bien, J. and Witten, D. (2022). Selective inference for hierarchical clustering. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 119, 332–342. doi:10.1080/01621459.2022.2116331

Chen, Y. T. and Witten, D. M. (2023). Selective inference for k-means clustering. Journal of Machine Learning Research, 24(152), 1–41. https://jmlr.org/papers/v24/22-0371.html

García Rasines, D. and Young, G. A. (2023). Splitting strategies for post-selection inference. Biometrika, 110(3), 597–614. doi:10.1093/biomet/asac070

Leiner, J., Duan, B., Wasserman, L. and Ramdas, A. (2023). Data fission: splitting a single data point. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 120(549), 135–146. doi:10.1080/01621459.2023.2270748

Neufeld, A., Dharamshi, A., Gao, L. L. and Witten, D. (2024). Data thinning for convolution-closed distributions. Journal of Machine Learning Research, 25(57), 1–35. https://jmlr.org/papers/v25/23-0446.html

See also

build_tessellation() and get_voronoi_seeds(), which accept this function's result directly as approx_n_cells and n (the first candidate is used, and the output records that it came from here; an NA from it stops them with a note on where it came from); assign_features_to_polygons() and summarize_by_cell() for the steps that follow.

Other aggregation: assign_features_to_polygons(), cell_values_at(), kriging_adequacy(), resolution_profile(), select_resolution(), summarize_by_cell(), summary.resolution_profile()

Examples

library(sf)
set.seed(1)
# Two clearly separated clusters: the elbow should sit near k = 2
pts <- st_as_sf(
  data.frame(x = 5e5 + c(runif(25, 0, 10), runif(25, 90, 100)),
             y = 5e6 + c(runif(25, 0, 10), runif(25, 90, 100))),
  coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32632
)
determine_optimal_levels(pts, max_levels = 6)   # 2 1 3: the elbow first
#> [1] 2 1 3
#> attr(,"structured")
#> [1] TRUE
#> attr(,"sag")
#> [1] 3.046636

# Points spread evenly have no elbow: NA, with structured = FALSE and a
# warning of class spatialkit_no_elbow that says why
even <- st_as_sf(data.frame(x = 5e5 + runif(200, 0, 100),
                            y = 5e6 + runif(200, 0, 100)),
                 coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32632)
determine_optimal_levels(even, max_levels = 6)
#> Warning: determine_optimal_levels(): the WSS curve has no elbow: on log-log axes it falls in a straight line, as it does for points with no cluster structure. k = 3 is where the chord rule lands on such a curve, set by the ladder (k = 1 to 6, max_levels) rather than by the data. Choose the count on other grounds, e.g. resolution_profile() with a response. Returning NA (on_no_elbow = "na").
#> [1] NA
#> attr(,"structured")
#> [1] FALSE
#> attr(,"sag")
#> [1] 0
